inclusion.rationale: The study makes dependence in literary text empirically inspectable while remaining separable from the later probabilistic-language-model spine.

significance.beginner: A short literary sequence can reveal that what comes next depends on what came immediately before.
significance.expert: The study estimates conditional vowel/consonant frequencies and compares observed dispersion with independent, simple-chain, and more complex chain assumptions.

limitations: The alphabet is collapsed to the binary classes vowel and consonant, discarding letter identity, words, syntax, and meaning.
The work does not train a predictor or present text generation as its objective.
Markov explicitly says the empirical example may not fully satisfy the theoretical assumptions.
The underlying Pushkin edition, exact terminal character, and a fully reproducible normalization pipeline are not specified.

uncertainties.note: The reviewed primary and historical sources do not document a direct Markov-to-Shannon influence path.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A primary source from Shannon or a participant would need to identify Markov’s text study as an influence.

inclusion.rationale: The paper brings discrete stochastic sources, conditional sequence probabilities, entropy, and constructed English approximations together in one inspectable formal account.

significance.beginner: Changing how much earlier text affects the next choice changes both the appearance and predictability of generated symbol sequences.
significance.expert: The paper represents written language as a discrete stochastic source, develops finite-state and n-gram conditionals, and relates longer contexts to conditional source entropy.

limitations: The paper is an engineering theory of communication and explicitly brackets semantic meaning from that engineering problem.
The English sequences are illustrative samples constructed from letter and word frequency information and book-based successor sampling, not learned neural models or evidence of comprehension.
Many discrete-source results use finite-state models and, unless stated otherwise, an ergodicity assumption; these idealizations should not be universalized.

inclusion.rationale: The paper turns contextual next-character predictability into an explicit experiment and connects ranked predictions to entropy bounds.

significance.beginner: A guessing experiment makes it possible to feel how preceding text narrows the plausible next character.
significance.expert: The paper estimates conditional character entropy from human rank predictions, separates observed prediction from an ideal conditional-probability ranking, and derives upper and lower bounds.

limitations: The experiments use human next-character prediction, not a trained language model, next-word task, or free-running generator.
The main context experiment draws from one literary source, permits reference aids, and does not report participant demographics or variability.
The long-context estimates use smoothed samples and apply an ideal-predictor lower bound to human rankings with an explicit approximation caveat.

uncertainties.note: The paper’s reported long-context condition and its N versus N-1 indexing should be preserved rather than silently normalized.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: The interface must show the paper’s labels and a separate normalized explanation.

works.title: Design of a Linguistic Statistical Decoder for the Recognition of Continuous Speech
works.displayCitation: F. Jelinek, L. R. Bahl, and R. L. Mercer, “Design of a Linguistic Statistical Decoder for the Recognition of Continuous Speech,” IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 21(3), 250–256 (May 1975).

dateEvidence.locator: IEEE Transactions on Information Theory volume 21, issue 3, May 1975

versions.title: Design of a Linguistic Statistical Decoder for the Recognition of Continuous Speech
versions.label: Original journal article

bibliography.citation: F. Jelinek, L. R. Bahl, and R. L. Mercer, “Design of a Linguistic Statistical Decoder for the Recognition of Continuous Speech,” IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 21(3), 250–256 (May 1975).

versions.notes: The manuscript-received day and the May 1975 journal issue are recorded as separate chronology events. The IBM archive’s 1 January catalog date is not used for ordering.

inclusion.rationale: The paper formulates a modular, corpus-estimated word-sequence probability within a factorized speech-decoding objective. It belongs as an engineering integration point on the statistical-ASR branch without being treated as the sole hinge in that broader line of work.

significance.beginner: When speech sounds are ambiguous, the decoder combines how well a candidate matches the sounds with how plausible its word sequence is in the domain.
significance.expert: The maximum-a-posteriori decoder factors Pr(W|A;L) into a language-model probability Pr(W|L) and a front-end likelihood Pr(A|W;L), then searches finite-state hypotheses by likelihood.

limitations: The article specifies a decoder that the IBM group planned to implement; it does not report end-to-end recognition accuracy or an experiment isolating the language-model contribution.
The target is carefully spoken speech in a relatively noiseless environment, with a roughly 10,000-word vocabulary and a two-million-word corpus of laser patent applications.

The decoder begins from a phonetic-symbol string supplied by a separate, speaker-trained acoustic processor rather than learning directly from waveforms; pronunciation and phonological probabilities are also speaker-dependent.
The instantiated language model uses explicit recent-word, part-of-speech, and content-class state features rather than learned distributed representations.
The paper leaves probability estimation for unseen language-model transitions under investigation.

Partial-hypothesis likelihoods use an approximation, and the described decoder scores the best state path while assuming that the loss relative to marginalizing all paths for a word sequence is negligible.
The work concerns speech transcription and does not present the language model as a standalone text generator.

uncertainties.note: The paper uses an information-theoretic framing but does not cite Shannon’s 1948 or 1951 papers; the atlas therefore records mechanism continuity without asserting paper-specific influence.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A source explicitly naming Shannon’s 1948 or 1951 paper as an influence would be required to document a paper-specific path.

uncertainties.note: The explanatory weight of this design article relative to its companion 1975 channel-decoding paper and Jelinek’s broader 1976 treatment has not yet received a claim-level comparison.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Compare the three primary texts before considering whether one should represent the statistical-ASR branch as a core hinge.

bibliography.citation: F. Jelinek and R. L. Mercer, “Interpolated Estimation of Markov Source Parameters from Sparse Data,” in E. S. Gelsema and L. N. Kanal, eds., Pattern Recognition in Practice: Proceedings of an International Workshop Held in Amsterdam, May 21–23, 1980, 381–397 (Amsterdam: North-Holland, 1980).
bibliography.venue: Pattern Recognition in Practice: Proceedings of an International Workshop Held in Amsterdam, May 21–23, 1980

versions.notes: The proceedings year is supported at year precision. The workshop dates belong to the volume title; the paper’s presentation day and a more precise proceedings publication date have not been established.

inclusion.rationale: The paper turns sparse Markov transition estimation into an explicit prediction problem, combines detailed and tied estimates by interpolation, and develops held-out and deleted procedures for testing the combination on data treated as unseen. It belongs as a statistical-estimation branch without being treated as a text-only or neural language model.

significance.beginner: A transition missing from a finite sample is not necessarily impossible, so the estimator blends a specific but fragile estimate with a broader estimate whose evidence is stronger.
significance.expert: The paper linearly interpolates detailed and tied Forward–Backward transition estimates, fits reliability-dependent weights on held-out or deleted blocks, and gives fixed and relaxed deleted-interpolation procedures.

limitations: The method is formulated for general finite-state Markov sources, including null transitions; the paper does not present the recursive higher-order-to-lower-order word n-gram equation commonly associated with later Jelinek–Mercer language-model smoothing.
The model structure and state-tying design are supplied by the experimenter, while the paper notes that a real generator’s structure is normally unknown and can be too large.
The held-out split size, deletion-block length, occupancy thresholds, state tying, and initial transition distributions are unresolved design choices that depend on the modeled situation.

The fixed deleted procedure uses a computational shortcut whose component estimates still depend implicitly on all data; the paper says separate per-block Forward–Backward runs would avoid it at higher cost.

The abstract reports simulations and successful speech-process applications, but the chapter gives no simulation table, dataset specification, quantitative comparison, or recognition metric from which to reconstruct those results.
The work estimates finite-state transition probabilities and does not learn distributed representations or a standalone text generator.

uncertainties.note: The National Diet Library record and the inspected chapter give pp. 381–397, ending with the complete reference list. J-GLOBAL additionally indexes pp. 401–402, whose content and relation to the chapter were not available for inspection.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Inspect the complete proceedings volume at pp. 398–402 to determine whether pp. 401–402 are discussion pages associated with this contribution.

uncertainties.note: The 1980 bibliography does not cite the 1975 decoder paper; it cites a different, then-forthcoming chapter by Jelinek, Mercer, and Bahl. The atlas therefore relates the two works editorially rather than as documented paper-specific influence.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A contemporary citation or participant source explicitly connecting the two papers would be required to upgrade the relationship evidence class.

uncertainties.note: The abstract’s simulation and speech-application claims cannot be evaluated quantitatively from the inspected chapter.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Locate the referenced experiment report or associated proceedings discussion with enough detail to identify the data, comparison, and result.

versions.notes: The corpus groups this bibliographically separate article as a companion version because every promoted lineage claim is present in both publications with the same section and equation numbering and substantially the same wording. This is an editorial deduplication decision, not an assertion that the authors or publishers designated the article as a revision or that either publication derived from the other. The article reports receipt on 23 February 1981 and revision on 28 September 1982, while the handbook publication is known only to year precision.

inclusion.rationale: The canonical chapter applies sparse-transition interpolation to a named trigram language model, reports how often unseen trigrams recur in new text, and gives a concrete deleted-estimation procedure. It supplies a word-trigram instantiation of the general 1980 estimator while remaining a broad speech-recognition survey rather than a standalone general-purpose language-model paper. Claim-level comparison found the same eight promoted lineage claims in the differently titled 1983 journal article, so that publication is recorded as a companion version rather than a second lineage node.

significance.beginner: Even a corpus of 1.5 million words leaves plausible three-word patterns unseen, so the chapter blends a fragile specific estimate with a broader one and chooses the balance using text treated as new.
significance.expert: The chapter maps the sparse-data failure to an IBM Laser Patent Text trigram model, applies equation (8.1) to detailed and tied transition estimates, and estimates reliability-bucketed mixture weights by deleted blocks.

limitations: The concrete language-model example is the domain-specific IBM Laser Patent Text corpus inside a continuous-speech-recognition survey; it is not evidence about unrestricted modern text.
The reported 23% unseen-trigram share is not reconstructible from the chapter passage because the new-text sample, its size, and the evaluation protocol are not specified there.

Equation (8.1) blends detailed and tied transition estimates; the inspected section does not present the compact recursive trigram-to-bigram-to-unigram notation associated with later descriptions of Jelinek–Mercer smoothing.
The chapter discusses a statistical language component within a larger speech system and does not learn distributed representations, semantics, or long-context dependencies.
The chapter is a broad survey of the IBM continuous-speech-recognition program; its atlas inclusion is limited to the sourced trigram and deleted-interpolation bridge.

Grouping the differently titled 1983 article, with its different author order, as a companion version is an editorial deduplication choice. It does not assert that the authors or publishers designated it as an edition, reprint, or derivative.

uncertainties.note: No authoritative publication month or day was found; some retrospective platform records show later dates that conflict with the 1982 volume.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A dated North-Holland publication notice or equivalent contemporary record would be required to refine the chronology beyond year precision.

uncertainties.note: The chapter passage does not identify the new text samples or expose enough counts to reproduce its reported 23% unseen-trigram share.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Locate the cited Laser Patent Text experiment report or underlying corpus protocol with sample definitions and counts.

uncertainties.note: The 1980 paper cites this chapter as forthcoming, while this chapter cites the 1980 paper for the detailed method; the reciprocal cross-references show overlapping preparation but do not establish the works’ development order.

All eight promoted lineage claims are present in both publications with matching section structure, equation numbering, quantitative values, and substantially the same wording; the 1983 article supplies no separate claim needed by the current LLM-lineage slice.

No inspected source labels the 1983 article an edition or reprint of the chapter. Its 23 February 1981 receipt and 28 September 1982 revision dates, combined with the chapter’s year-only publication date, do not establish either text’s development order.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A contemporary draft history, publisher statement, correspondence, or specific participant account would be required to replace the editorial companion grouping with a documented version or derivation relationship.

ideas.name: Text as a dependent sequence
ideas.description: Adjacent symbol classes in observed text can have different conditional frequencies than independence would predict.

uncertainties.note: The opening treatment is intentionally limited to the vowel/consonant abstraction used in the 1913 study.

ideas.name: Language as a conditional stochastic source
ideas.description: A discrete language source emits successive symbols according to probabilities that may depend on preceding choices.

ideas.name: Entropy as sequence uncertainty
ideas.description: Conditional entropy quantifies average uncertainty about a next event when contextual information is known.

ideas.name: Increasing-order language approximation
ideas.description: Successively longer conditional contexts can produce samples with more of a language’s local statistical structure.

uncertainties.note: Order labels in the paper are preserved alongside explicit context length because they differ from some modern conventions.

ideas.name: Contextual next-symbol prediction
ideas.description: The predictability of the next character can be studied while the correct preceding text remains visible.

ideas.name: Prediction-based entropy bounds
ideas.description: The rank frequencies of next-character predictions can be related to upper and lower bounds on conditional entropy.

ideas.name: Language-model-guided decoding
ideas.description: A decoder can rank candidate word sequences by combining their language-model probability with the likelihood of the observed signal.

ideas.name: Corpus-estimated language model
ideas.description: A structured sequence model can obtain transition probabilities from counts over a domain corpus.

ideas.name: Sparse language-model estimation
ideas.description: A finite sample can leave plausible sequence transitions with zero observed or expected counts, so an estimated probability of zero need not mark an impossible transition.

ideas.name: Interpolated transition estimation
ideas.description: A transition estimate can blend a detailed distribution with a more broadly tied distribution, with the mixing weight reflecting their relative reliability.

ideas.name: Deleted estimation
ideas.description: A block is evaluated as if unseen while estimation is intended to rely on retained observations, making the tuning target resemble future prediction more closely than training-data fit; practical shortcuts can retain implicit full-data dependence.

ideas.name: Word-trigram language modeling
ideas.description: A corpus-derived trigram model assigns probabilities to local three-word patterns, but finite training data leave many patterns unobserved even at million-word scale.

uncertainties.note: The idea is scoped to the chapter’s Laser Patent Text example and is not treated as evidence about unrestricted corpora.

claims.statement: Under stated continuity, equiprobable-choice, and grouping assumptions, Shannon obtains the form H = -K Σ p log p and calls it the entropy of a probability distribution.

evidence.support: States the assumptions, the entropy form, and its interpretation as information, choice, or uncertainty.

limitations: Shannon presents the characterization theorem as plausibility for later definitions, not as a prerequisite for the rest of the theory.

claims.statement: The paper defines conditional entropy as average remaining uncertainty and states that knowing another event cannot increase that uncertainty.

evidence.support: Defines Hx(y), gives the joint-entropy decomposition, and compares conditional with unconditional uncertainty.

limitations: Conditional entropy here is not itself the modern neural cross-entropy training objective.

claims.statement: For the stationary-source treatment, Shannon defines F_N as the entropy of the Nth symbol conditioned on the preceding N−1 symbols and shows that F_N is non-increasing with N and approaches the source entropy.

evidence.support: Defines F_N using N−1 preceding symbols, proves its monotonic behavior, and relates its limit to source entropy.

limitations: The paper’s N counts the predicted symbol, so the conditioning context has length N−1.

claims.statement: The 1951 method studies how well a next letter can be predicted when preceding text is known and combines experimental prediction with theoretical analysis to bound entropy.

evidence.support: States the next-letter task, preceding-context condition, and upper/lower-bound purpose.

limitations: The task concerns characters in printed English, not word tokens.

claims.statement: In the prediction protocol, a subject guesses the next character of an unfamiliar passage and receives the correct character before proceeding, so later guesses always use the correct prefix.

evidence.support: Describes both the single-guess and repeated-guess versions and the feedback supplied after errors.

limitations: Prediction errors do not propagate into subsequent context.
The repeated-guess rank result must not be conflated with the separate single-guess illustration.

claims.statement: The main context experiment uses 100 randomly selected 15-character samples from Jefferson the Virginian, tests conditions with up to 14 preceding characters plus a reported long-context condition, and permits specified frequency tables, word lists, and a dictionary.

evidence.support: Describes the sampling frame, context conditions, source book, and aids available to the subject.

limitations: The first two Table I columns are calculated from frequency tables rather than observed in the human experiment.
The paper’s N and N-1 labels and its long-context column should be preserved rather than silently normalized.

claims.statement: Shannon reports that, apart from statistical fluctuations, the Table I predictions generally improve as the subject receives more knowledge of the preceding text.

evidence.support: States the observed context-versus-prediction trend and explicitly qualifies it for statistical fluctuation.

limitations: This trend is reported for the paper’s small human-prediction experiment and should not be generalized without its sampling caveat.

claims.statement: For the theoretical ideal predictor, possible next letters are ordered by decreasing true conditional probability given the preceding context, and the observed letter is represented by its rank.

evidence.support: Defines optimal conditional-probability ordering and rank encoding for the ideal predictor.

limitations: The ideal predictor is a theoretical oracle-like construction, not a trained machine.

claims.statement: The frequencies of correct-letter prediction ranks are used to derive upper and lower bounds on N-gram conditional entropy.

evidence.support: Gives the inequality connecting rank frequencies with upper and lower entropy bounds.

limitations: The lower-bound derivation assumes ideal conditional-probability ranking.

evidence.support: States the sampling-error and human-versus-ideal-prediction qualifications.

claims.statement: The proposed linguistic statistical decoder takes a phonetic-symbol string from an acoustic processor and searches for the most likely input sentence through a statistical language model, pronunciation modeling, phonetic matching, and word-level search control.

claims.statement: For acoustic observation A and language L, the decoder ranks word sequences W by Pr(W|A;L), factoring the posterior into the language-model probability Pr(W|L) and front-end likelihood Pr(A|W;L), with the denominator Pr(A|L) independent of W.

limitations: The probability identity defines the ranking criterion; it does not establish that the component models are well estimated.

claims.statement: For an incomplete sentence hypothesis, the decoder replaces the exact remainder-output probability with a Markov approximation based on observed front-end output, so the paper states that the resulting likelihood is no longer exact.

claims.statement: A word-sequence likelihood would sum the likelihoods of every state sequence yielding those words, but the described decoder selects the most likely word-and-part-of-speech state sequence and the authors state that they expect the resulting performance loss to be negligible.

evidence.support: Contrasts marginal word-sequence likelihood with state-sequence selection and labels the expected loss as the authors’ belief.

limitations: The negligible-loss expectation is not supported by a reported recognition comparison in this paper.

learningObjectives.objective: Explain in plain language why different next-vowel rates after vowels and consonants show local dependence without turning the study into a modern language model.
learningObjectives.successCriterion: The learner can contrast independence with conditional frequency and name at least one limit of the binary abstraction.

learningObjectives.objective: Reconstruct the one- and two-predecessor conditional estimates and compare the reported dispersion values without claiming an exact Markov order or modern significance test.
learningObjectives.successCriterion: The learner can reproduce the conditional rates and state why the paper’s model-fit conclusion remains qualified.

learningObjectives.objective: Describe how adding local context changes the next-symbol choices and the visible structure of Shannon’s English approximations.
learningObjectives.successCriterion: The learner can distinguish independent sampling from a context-conditioned next-symbol choice and avoids equating resemblance with understanding.

learningObjectives.objective: Relate the discrete-source and n-gram constructions to conditional entropy F_N while preserving Shannon’s order convention and modeling assumptions.
learningObjectives.successCriterion: The learner can map a context length to its conditional distribution and explain why longer context cannot increase ideal conditional uncertainty.

learningObjectives.objective: Use the letter-guessing protocol to connect more informative preceding text with fewer plausible next characters and lower uncertainty.
learningObjectives.successCriterion: The learner can describe the feedback protocol and explain why guesses always use the correct prefix.

learningObjectives.objective: Separate human rank observations from the ideal conditional-probability predictor and trace how rank frequencies enter the reported entropy bounds.
learningObjectives.successCriterion: The learner can identify which bound depends on ideal ranking and enumerate the main sampling and protocol caveats.

learningObjectives.objective: Explain why an ambiguous speech transcription can change when the decoder considers both sound fit and the plausibility of a word sequence, without treating the language model as if it hears audio.

learningObjectives.successCriterion: Given an ambiguous phonetic input, the learner can separate acoustic fit from sequence plausibility and name one domain limit of the model.

learningObjectives.objective: Trace the posterior factorization through the finite-state language probability and likelihood-ordered search, distinguish the unresolved sparse-count estimation problem, and identify where partial-hypothesis scoring and state-path selection depart from exact word-sequence inference.
learningObjectives.successCriterion: The learner can separate the language prior, front-end likelihood, normalization, transition estimation, and two search approximations while preserving the paper’s stated scope.

learningObjectives.objective: Explain why a transition absent from a finite sample need not be impossible, why a fragile specific estimate can share weight with a broader estimate, and why that blend should be judged on observations treated as new.
learningObjectives.successCriterion: Given high- and low-evidence states, the learner can choose the direction in which λ should move and explain why zero observations do not by themselves prove impossibility.

learningObjectives.objective: Derive the equation (18) mixture, distinguish held-out, fixed-deleted, shortcut, and relaxed procedures, and identify which structural settings and empirical claims remain unresolved.

learningObjectives.objective: Explain why a million-word corpus can still miss plausible three-word patterns, how an exact word pair can borrow evidence by generalizing its earlier word and then both words to parts of speech, and why the borrowing strength is learned on text treated as new.
